core: Ancient Egyptian art as historically changing practices across a long sequence of periods, not a single fixed style
How material, scale, setting, inscriptions, and visual conventions can guide careful analysis
Distinct roles of works associated with tombs, temples, royal settings, and daily life
supporting: Registers, composite viewpoints, proportional systems, and hierarchical scale as visual conventions that require contextual interpretation
The relationship of some funerary images and objects to beliefs and ritual preparations for the afterlife
The importance of specific date, period, site, and object record when discussing an Egyptian work
outOfScope: A complete dynastic chronology, catalogue of deities, hieroglyphic grammar, or full history of Egyptian religion
Detailed instruction on pyramids, mummification, temple architecture, particular rulers, or individual works
Claims that every Egyptian work was funerary, that every image had one fixed meaning, or that artistic conventions never changed
Modern ownership, museum collecting, repatriation, appraisal, authentication, or legal advice

claims.claim: Ancient Egyptian art spans a long and internally varied history; period, site, medium, and setting are needed to make a precise claim about an individual work.

Some Egyptian images use conventions such as registers, a proportional grid, and hierarchical scale, but these are analytical prompts rather than evidence of an unchanging style or one meaning in every context.

Many surviving Egyptian works come from tomb settings and can inform study of funerary practices, but tomb evidence is also selective and must not stand for all Egyptian art or all Egyptians' experiences.
A tomb, temple, or object record can provide evidence about setting, material, date, and documented use; visible form alone does not prove an artist's private intention or an exact ritual meaning.
Ancient Egyptian artists worked across media including stone, wood, paint, metal, ceramic, and faience, and material choices affect both production and survival.

In ancient Egyptian funerary contexts, particular images, texts, and objects could be connected to ritual provisions and hopes for continued existence after death, but a work should be interpreted through its own documented context.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Older survey descriptions often present Egyptian art as stylistically unchanging or reduce it to tomb art.
positions: Repeated conventions can be observed across particular periods and settings, and funerary evidence is especially visible in many collections.
The long history of Egypt includes changing periods, materials, patrons, settings, and visual decisions; surviving tomb evidence is not a complete sample.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses named visual conventions only as evidence-based descriptive tools, then requires an object-specific period and setting. It treats funerary material as one documented context among several rather than a universal explanation.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft supplied no history, evidence, artistic context, or distinction between ancient Egypt's many periods and settings.
Its vocabulary was circular, its explanation was generic, its analogy lacked a limit, and its three quick-check items did not meet the required four-option format.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with a source-grounded introduction to historical specificity, visual conventions, material, and context.
Corrected the implied singularity of 'Egyptian art' by distinguishing periods and tomb, temple, royal, and other settings.
Added a worked example that separates observation, documented context, and cautious inference.
Rebuilt the assessment as five original four-option questions across recall, understanding, application, and analysis.
rightsIssues: The Met educator resource and Timeline essay are used as REFERENCE_ONLY institutional scholarship; no source prose or images are reproduced.
Smarthistory is used as a REFERENCE_ONLY open educational source; all lesson prose, scenarios, and questions are original.

sourceRecords.title: The Art of Ancient Egypt: A Resource for Educators
sourceRecords.notes: Read as an authoritative museum education resource. It supports the lesson's chronological framing, multiple media, selected visual conventions, and the functions of some funerary material. It is used for verified facts and instructional framing only; no source wording or image is adapted.

sourceRecords.title: The World of Ancient Egypt
sourceRecords.notes: Read as a Tier B open educational overview. It supports discussion of canon grids, hierarchical scale, and Egyptian visual conventions within historical context. The lesson does not treat its examples as universal rules, and all prose and questions are original.

sourceRecords.title: Egyptian Tombs: Life Along the Nile
sourceRecords.notes: Read as museum scholarship on excavated nonroyal tombs in western Thebes and their materials. It supports the importance of documented tomb context and the way tombs provide valuable but partial evidence for past lives and funerary practice.
